Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round

CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel. Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc. 3 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they

title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)
text: engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment. The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. It should advance the state-of-the-art in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation, which can be more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 2012). Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity

title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)
text: = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment. Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide this environment. 5 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 C. text: the ‘Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 1. Plan and support flight testing on the ISS. 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. In contrast to objective 2 (and hypothesis 3), it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate. 3. As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE

text: concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning. 7 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the CFI-G investigation and the second-round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (sFlame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel,

For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 8 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.

ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Lightemitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction

A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements. All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and that data is not missing. While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 10 tests typically completed per day. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation

A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines. H. title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)
text: in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes. 28 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI-G. Furthermore, the CFI-G tests were conducted using the 29 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. text: is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, nonpremixed cool flames can be directly by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. text: the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. A challenge for cool flame detection is concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes. 35 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion

title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)
text: In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. VI. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). Mission anomalies On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU-G, also known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working. Among them, 189 flames experienced radiative extinction, and the rest were extinguished when their flow was terminated, either because the preset flow time was out or the burner overheated. Of those that extinguished radiatively, 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames. These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% nbutane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s. Cool diffusion flames were initially identified by the readings of radiometers after the radiative extinction of hot flames. Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped flowing. Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot-cool flame transitions. The first cool flame, the first drop of the radiant heat flux, followed the radiative extinction of the first hot flame. In a few seconds, the heat flux abruptly increased due to reignition of a hot flame. This cycle of radiative extinction, transition to a cool flame, and reignition of a hot flame continued until the flow was terminated. The observed cool flames are summarized in Table 3. Cool flames were also identified by processed images taken from the intensified camera. When cool flames appeared after the radiative extinction of the hot flames, no flame luminosity was evident for about 1 s, after which cool flames appeared. For test points 21174C3, C4, C6, and F1, the cool flames lasted for approximately 14 s and disappeared as soon as the fuel flow stopped. Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to normal gravity. Week 11: June 18-24 On GMT 174, we ignited 16 nitrogen-diluted butane flames in the final tests for the first round of ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Cool flames remained elusive, where there has been no clear evidence of these low-temperature phenomena during this round of testing. In the coming weeks and months, we will review the data more closely to assess their potential presence. Regardless, we gathered a wealth of valuable data that will improve our fundamental understanding of soot process and flame dynamics. Since CFI-G tested with different fuels, these data expand upon the results gained from the other ACME experiments. Next week, the ACME Chamber Insert will be configured to support the second and final round of CFI-G testing. This testing will explore the potential existence of cool flames in an inverse configuration. The flow direction will be reversed, where a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen will flow from the burner into the Combustion Chamber, which will be filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel. As a result, the flames will be inside out, where, as an example, the soot will be formed outside of the flame. 57 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again due to heat loss. This repeated opening and closing of the flame creates a visually dramatic flame that swirls around the porous spherical burner. Second round (inverse flames except for the final test day) Week 12: June 25 – July 1 Recent data analysis shows evidence of cool flames! Data from several of the ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) tests on GMT 174 indicate the presence of cool flames. These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogendiluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after the hot flames quenched. Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were discovered in 2012 with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. Now, we’ve achieved non-premixed cool flames using gaseous fuels! Cool flame chemistry is important to ignition and the results could lead to vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution. Figure 1. The oxygen flows outward until it reaches sufficient fuel to be consumed. As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames. The oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent in this trio of tests. These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame. The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens of seconds. Meanwhile, some flames are quasi-steady despite the opening. This is one example of how these spherical flames are not as simple as had earlier been imagined. text: IN THIS LOG This clip from the beginning of a test point video shows an inverse flame that is initially sooty, but the soot quickly fades away as the flame temperature drops. With inverse flames, the fuel is outside the flame, so that is where the soot forms. Soot is created when the fuel in the chamber, heated to a high temperature by the flame, combines in the absence of oxygen, which is inside the flame. The flame cools due to both radiative heat loss and conductive heat loss to the burner, especially to the tube supplying the oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The soot lasts the longest away from the supply tube where the flame is hottest. To visibly glow due to their temperature, materials must 62 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 be about 800 K. Therefore, if it’s not hot enough for soot to glow, then it’s also not hot enough for the fuel to combine and then form the soot. Week of April 26, 2021 Observing flames The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) include six independent studies of flames that seek to improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollution from combustion on Earth and help prevent fires in spacecraft. ACME investigations are conducted in the space station’s Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which includes a combustion chamber, gas bottles, and five cameras for observing flames. The research aimed at spacecraft fire prevention examines different materials, including how to put them out when burning, conditions needed for a material to continue burning, and the effectiveness of existing methods to screen and select materials for spacecraft. The crew replaced controllers for ACME during the week. Week of October 11, 2021 Coolest flames in space The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is a set of six independent studies of gaseous flames conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The researchers’ goals are to gain information that can lead to improved fuel efficiency, reduced pollutant production in practical combustion on Earth, and improved spacecraft fire prevention. One of the ACME studies currently being conducted is known as the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. A cool flame is one that burns at about 600 degrees Celsius. A candle is about two times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius. The results of this investigation could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. text: the ISS data collection The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI). 86 ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 Appendix N. Introduction The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that is sufficient for informed interpretation of the experimental results. In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects may be briefly addressed. The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station (ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and ethylene. In addition to the fuel state, the current ACME experiments use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017. The facility was reconfigured and set up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 25 astronauts from Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s research. As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that began in Nov. 2017. It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various documents, such as those listed below. These are listed in reverse chronological order, where the

The CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia. In 1997, the combustion research facility was within Spacelab on the STS-83 and STS-94 (Microgravity Science Laboratory) missions. It was subsequently reconfigured and flew in 2003 within SPACEHAB, again in the shuttle’s payload bay, in the STS-107 mission. The Combustion Module investigations included Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL), and the Water-Mist Fire Suppression Experiment (Mist). Although all three experiments burned gaseous fuel, each had its own chamber insert, whereas ACME features a single modular chamber insert to accomplish multiple investigations. A significant difference between the CIR and its shuttle precursor is that the ISS tests are remotely commanded from the ground without crew involvement, which wasn’t the case with the Combustion Module research. But in all cases the crew are required to configure the necessary hardware. Engineering Overview A. General Description This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16– 18 March 2014. IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately describe the final engineering in some regards. Therefore updates, clarifications, additional details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped. As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 5 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: which is for data acquisition and control. Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 5 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning. Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are addressed in detail in section 3.C. Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching. Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the exception of the latter’s first day testing. The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip. For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 6 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately,

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Lightemitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame conditions. The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction. The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is 7 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions. For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A). Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras. Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second (fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. Gas-Jet Burners The fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm, where two spaceflight copies of each were fabricated because of concerns that they might be damaged. However, only a single copy of the larger diameter burner has thus far been used during the spaceflight tests, where that use was limited to the second round of the E-FIELD Flames testing. The same commercial stainless-steel tubing used for the coflow burner’s inner tube was also used for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner. Meanwhile, the nominal outer diameter (OD) was 2.41 mm, again for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner and the inner tube of the coflow burner. The stainless-steel fuel tube in the burner has inner and outer diameter of 2.16 and 2.41 mm, respectively. Spherical Burners The spherical burners have thus far been used for the CFI-G, Flame Design, and s-Flame experiments. In contrast to initial plans, spaceflight burners were only fabricated with a 6.35-mm porous sphere. It was initially expected that flames which were more spherical might be generated with larger diameter porous spheres, but 2.2-s drop testing indicated that 6.35-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating spherical flames. Multiple copies of the spherical burner were launched to the ISS because of concerns that they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently spherically symmetric. The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6

title: ACME Engineering Implementation (2022)
text: were launched to the ISS because of concerns that they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently spherically symmetric. The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6 g/cm3. More specifically, each sphere was formed by sintering together sintered disks, where the supply tube should extend to the sphere’s center. Neglecting the interior of the supply tube, there is presumably no cavity within the porous sphere. Each sphere was furthermore sinter-bonded to its stainless-steel supply tube. As a side effect, the tubing lost its temper and became very pliable because of the high temperature required for the bonding. Therefore, a close-fitting support tube, with an outer diameter of 1.8 mm, was added to the design. It doesn’t quite extend to the porous sphere as can be seen in Figure 46. The gap between the support tube and the burner is often obvious in flame imaging because the supply tube is more reflective than the support tube. Each burner was equipped with an extremely fine, sheathed, type-K thermocouple which was embedded as much as ~1 mm into the porous sphere. The thermocouple hole was 0.76 to 1.0 mm deep (and 0.25-0.30 mm in diameter) where the thermocouple was meant to be inserted fully, i.e., until reaching the hole’s bottom, but that may not be its exact position. The junction is of course not at the extreme end of the sheathed thermocouple, but it is very fine and presumably close. If the porous sphere is imagined as a globe with the supply tube as the south pole, the thermocouple is inserted in the lower hemisphere, between the equator and pole as seen in Figure 46. 43 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 Figure 46. The spherical burners were first used for the Flame Design experiment, where the first flame tests were conducted on 25 April 2019. However, after several days of testing it was concluded by the investigators that the flames were insufficiently symmetric at high burner flow rates to meet the science objectives. At the high flow rates, the flame ceased to be spherically symmetric and its center didn’t coincide with the burner’s center. The results indicate that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube was more porous than the sintered sphere itself, where the flame was shifted toward the supply tube. Therefore, the spherical burner was replaced on 14 June 2019 where the shift was from serial number 1002 to 1003. The subsequent burner (s/n 1003) showed similar behavior, but to a significantly reduced degree. As a result, some of the early Flame Design testing was repeated after the burner swap. This burner (s/n 1003) has thus far been used for all subsequent spherical flame testing including the tests for the s-Flame and CFIG experiments. 44 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 4. Igniter Tips Two types of crew-exchangeable igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests were conducted with a tip featuring a simple loop of Kanthal A-1 wire (0.25 mm in diameter) which was resistively heated with specification of the voltage and duration. A pre-heat voltage and duration, e.g., prior to burner flow, can also be specified. The second type features a small coil of Kanthal A-1 wire (0.32 mm in diameter), where it was used in the final six s-Flame test days (in June-July 2020) and throughout the second round of BRE testing (in Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021). The two innermost thermocouples (i.e., closest to the spherical burner) on each rake are type-B, while the outer thermocouples are type-K. In contrast, only the two thermocouples at 13 and 25 mm were intended to be type B, where this discrepancy is documented in deviation ACME-DEV026. There are also two separate thermocouples which are each at nominally 200 mm distance from the center of the spherical burner where these have thus far been always installed. However, they are located far upstream of the burner outlets and as such will be of limited value for experiments with the other burner types. Thermocouple 2 (at 200 mm, on the relay side) was reported to be bent by about 10 degrees on 3 April 2018, about 10-15 degrees on 22 May 2018, and about 30 degrees on 19 June 2018. The next three reports indicated the same bend, and the procedures were changed to cover the tip 63 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 during crew operations. Photographs, where an example is shown in Figure 70, and crew inspection indicate that has remained bent about 30 degrees since that time. Given the 5 mm length of the bent exposed thermocouple tip, the effect on the 200 mm distance to the spherical burner center is small. Figure 70. The chamber was dark and only the ignitor, with a halogen bulb instead of the ignitor wire, was powered at a setting close to the expected max. The resulting image shows the spherical burner is in the center (it is dark but can be seen) and the bright ignitor is coming in from the left. Between the 2 you can see the round reflection off the window directly opposite from the Data Camera. Note that the opposite window is the Intensified Camera view, looking at the flame from the other side. There are no other significant internal reflections from the hardware, leaving the only concern for reflections being the opposite window. Deviations and waivers which were identified by Stocker as affecting science in August 2016 are topically listed here. The degree to which the deviations and waivers were expected to positively or adversely affect the science at that time is indicated using stoplight indicators for good (G), neutral (N), cautionary (Y), or bad (R). The issue of back-reflection from opposed windows noted in regard to ACME-WAI-048 was subsequently addressed with the addition of internal window covers shown in the figures in section 3.C Optical Layout. Meanwhile, ignition concerns associated with ACME-WAI-019 were partially mitigated by the development of a second type of hot-wire igniter tip, specifically with a spring-like coil design. Internet Links These websites may be useful for understanding ACME’s engineering implementation and interpreting the experimental results. ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments CIR Combustion Integrated Rack (ISS facility in which the ACME experiments were conducted) 100 ACME Engineering Implementation 19 May 2022 Short videos clips providing overviews of the ACME chamber insert and research can be seen and downloaded. Meanwhile, a time-lapse video clip showing astronaut Paolo Nespoli (ESA) reconfiguring the CIR’s optics bench for initial ACME testing can be seen and downloaded. As mentioned in the previous section, photographs of the hardware and more can be seen at: www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames www.facebook.com/space.flames These Space Flames websites are about space-based studies of combustion in general, but they are administered by Dennis Stocker, the ACME Project Scientist, and are an excellent source of photos of the ACME hardware and crew operations. 8.
